query: What are the hazards at conveyor transfer points and what safety devices or actions are relevant?

text_chunks.title: Instrumentation & Safety Devices on the Conveyor
text_chunks.content: Instrumentation & Safety Devices on the Conveyor Think of instrumentation as the conveyor's nervous system — sensors spread across the full length that continuously sense abnormal conditions and either warn operators or automatically stop the machine before a small problem becomes a catastrophe. A belt conveyor in a modern Coal Handling Plant is fitted with numerous sensors, switches, and protective devices along its entire length. These are not optional extras — they are mandatory safety and operational requirements under Indian Electricity Rules, factory safety regulations, and plant operating procedures. As an intern, you will see these devices everywhere on the conveyor. Knowing what each one does is essential. MOVING BELT TAIL PULLEY DRIVE PULLEY M ━━ EMERGENCY PULL CORD (Both Sides, Full Length) ━━ EPC EPC EPC BSW Belt Sway Switch BSW ZSS SPD Zero Speed / Underspeed Switch BW WEIGH Belt Weigher (Load cell) CBD CHUTE Chute Blocked Detector 🔥 Thermal/ Fire Detector Return Strand EPC = Emergency Pull Cord BSW = Belt Sway Switch ZSS = Zero Speed Switch BW = Belt Weigher CBD = Chute Blocked Detector 🔥 = Fire Detector

text_chunks.title: Transfer Points & Flow Behaviour
text_chunks.content: Transfer Points & Flow Behaviour A transfer point is like a controlled handover baton pass — coal must land precisely on the next belt. Any miss, blockage, or misalignment at this point disrupts the entire downstream flow. Wherever coal moves from one conveyor to the next — or from a hopper to a conveyor — there is a transfer point . These are not minor connections; they are among the most critical and most hazardous locations in the entire Coal Handling Plant. Understanding what happens at a transfer point is essential before entering the CHP. BC-1 (Upper Conveyor) Coal on BC-1 Head Pulley TRANSFER CHUTE (guides coal) ↓ Coal falls here BC-2 (Lower Conveyor) Impact Zone Coal on BC-2 ⚠ DUST ⚠ Spillage ⚠ Spillage ⚠ BLOCKAGE RISK Wet/sticky coal can block chute Coal must land centrally on BC-2 belt. Any deviation → spillage or belt drift.

text_chunks.title: What Can Go Wrong at a Transfer Point
text_chunks.content: What Can Go Wrong at a Transfer Point Problem | Cause | Consequence ; Chute Blockage | Wet, fine, or sticky coal accumulates inside the chute and sticks to walls, eventually bridging across. | Coal backs up onto BC-1, causing it to overload. If blockage is not cleared quickly, the conveyor trips. ; Spillage | Coal falls outside the belt edges due to misaligned chute, worn skirt boards, or over-speed discharge. | Accumulation of coal on walkways and structure — slipping hazard, fire risk from dust, structural overloading. ; Dust Generation | Free-fall of coal creates turbulent air that carries fine coal particles. Longer drop height = more dust. | Respiratory hazard, reduced visibility, fire and explosion risk from coal dust cloud. ; Belt Damage at Impact | Large coal lumps falling from height impact the belt at the transfer point, especially if impact idlers are worn. | Belt cover damage, gouging, or even belt puncture — leading to belt failure. ; Off-centre Loading | Coal does not land centrally on BC-2 due to incorrect chute alignment or spillage plate wear. | Belt drifts to one side → edge damage → spillage → potential belt damage against structure. Transfer towers are enclosed structures at junctions between conveyors. They are high-dust, confined-space environments with active machinery on multiple levels. Entry requires a Confined Space Entry Permit, dust mask, and must always be done with a buddy. Never enter during conveyor operation without a specific maintenance permit.

text_chunks.title: Safety Device Reference Guide

breadcrumb: Belt Conveyor Operation – L1 Foundational Course | CHP Training
Instrumentation & Safety Devices on the Conveyor

text_chunks.content: Safety Device Reference Guide Device | Location on Conveyor | Function | Response When Activated ; Emergency Pull Cord (EPC) | Both sides, full length of conveyor, approximately every 30–50 m | Allows any person anywhere along the conveyor to immediately stop it in an emergency by pulling the rope/wire | Immediate emergency stop of conveyor drive motor. Conveyor cannot restart until EPC is reset and root cause investigated. ; Belt Sway Switch (BSW) | Both sides, spaced every 50–75 m along carry and return strand | Detects lateral drift of the belt beyond a set limit. Has two positions: first position = alarm; second position = trip. | First activation: Alarm in control room. Second (greater drift): Conveyor trip. Prevents belt edge from contacting steel structure. ; Zero Speed Switch (ZSS) | Tail pulley shaft or on a return idler | Monitors belt speed. Detects if the belt has stopped (zero speed) while the motor is still running — indicating belt slip. | Conveyor trip + alarm. Prevents drive pulley from running against a stationary belt (which causes fire from friction). ; Belt Weigher (BW) | Fixed location on the conveyor, typically mid-span | Measures the weight of coal on the belt per unit length using load cells. Calculates instantaneous TPH and cumulative tonnes. | Data sent to control room / DCS. No trip — provides operational data. High load may trigger an alarm. ; Chute Blocked Detector (CBD) | Inside transfer chutes at transfer points | Detects when coal has accumulated and blocked the chute (using vibration probe, ultrasonic, or paddle switch). | Alarm in control room. May automatically stop upstream feeder to prevent further coal accumulation. ; Thermal / Fire Detector | Inside conveyor galleries (tunnels) and transfer towers | Detects elevated temperature indicating a developing fire. Linear heat detection cable runs along the belt gallery roof. | Fire alarm. Conveyor trip. Activation of fire suppression system (CO₂ or water mist). Control room alert. ; Underspeed Switch | Drive shaft area | Detects if belt is running slower than designed speed (but not zero). Indicates overloading or drive slip developing. | Alarm → trip if underspeed persists. Allows early intervention before full slippage occurs. ; Motor Overload Relay (OLR) | Motor control centre (MCC) / switchgear panel | Monitors motor current. If the motor draws current above the rated limit for a set time (indicating overload), it trips. | Motor trip + alarm. Conveyor stops. Investigation required to identify overload cause before restart. When you walk a conveyor on site, you will see red ropes, yellow boxes, and small switches mounted on the frame at regular intervals — these are all part of this safety system. You will hear terms like "BSW trip," "ZSS alarm," or "EPC activation" on the radio constantly. Now you know exactly what each term means, what triggered it, and what the plant team needs to do in response. On some plants, under production pressure, well-meaning but incorrect actions include bypassing a belt sway switch that keeps tripping, disabling a chute blocked detector that gives "false" alarms, or tying off an EPC that was accidentally pulled. This is an extremely dangerous practice. Every safety device bypass removes one layer of protection from the system. Multiple bypasses create a condition where a fatal accident can occur without any warning. As an intern, if you are ever asked to bypass a safety device, immediately consult your supervisor. Document it. Never accept it as routine.

text_chunks.title: Safety & Hazard Awareness

breadcrumb: Belt Conveyor Operation – L1 Foundational Course | CHP Training

text_chunks.content: Safety & Hazard Awareness Moving machinery + bulk material + confined spaces = continuous risk. Most conveyor accidents happen not because of complexity but because someone was not aware of where the danger was. You do not need to be doing anything wrong to be injured near a conveyor. You simply need to be in the wrong place, distracted, or unaware of what is moving around you. The conveyor does not slow down for you. It does not have a sensor that detects a human body near it. It will continue running at full speed regardless. Your awareness is your protection. MOVING BELT (entire length is a hazard) TAIL PULLEY 🔴 PINCH ZONE Entanglement risk DRIVE PULLEY 🔴 PINCH + NIP ZONE High-torque crush risk 🟠 FEED POINT Impact hazard Dust cloud 🟠 TRANSFER POINT Spillage, blockage Confined space 🟡 BELT SURFACE Never touch/step on moving belt 🟡 Return strand — carryback coal falls here — slip hazard below ☁ Dust cloud ☁ Dust cloud ━━━ Emergency Pull Cord (full length) — Pull anywhere to STOP conveyor ━━━ HAZARD ZONE LEGEND RED = Extreme danger (pinch/nip/crush) — Mandatory guarding required ORANGE = High hazard (spillage, blockage, dust, confined space) — Permit required YELLOW = Caution zone (moving belt, carryback, slipping) — Stay clear, PPE required

text_chunks.title: Hazard-by-Hazard Analysis
text_chunks.content: Hazard-by-Hazard Analysis Pulleys rotate continuously at high speed. The nip point — where the belt meets the pulley — has an extremely small gap that closes in milliseconds. A finger, loose clothing, or hair entering this gap will be drawn in with full motor force before any human reaction is possible. Guards (physical covers) must always be in place over all pulleys. If a guard is missing — report it immediately and do not approach the pulley. The belt surface itself is a hazard. Loose clothing, gloves, tools, or anything trailing near the belt can be instantly grabbed and pulled in. Belt speed (1.5–2.5 m/s) is faster than human reflex. This type of accident typically results in degloving injuries, crush injuries, or fatalities. Rule: always wear close-fitting PPE near conveyors. Never lean over a running belt. At transfer points, coal falls from one conveyor to the next. Large coal lumps weighing several kilograms can bounce or be thrown sideways if a blockage or imbalance occurs. Standing below or beside an active chute is extremely dangerous. Transfer towers also have open floors and structural walkways at multiple levels — falling coal from one level can injure personnel on a lower level. Fine coal dust generated at transfer points, feed points, and from carryback is a dual hazard. Respiratory: Coal dust causes coal worker's pneumoconiosis (CWP/"black lung") with long-term exposure. Always wear a P2/P3 dust mask in dusty areas. Fire: Coal dust suspended in air at concentrations above the Lower Explosive Limit (LEL) can ignite from a spark or hot surface. Accumulated coal dust on hot surfaces (like a seized idler or a slipping belt) can also self-ignite. Coal spillage on walkways creates an extremely slippery surface, especially when wet. Carryback coal falls from the return strand onto the floor below the conveyor. Structural platforms, stairs, and walkways in CHP are often narrow and positioned close to moving equipment. Falls from elevated walkways (transfer towers can be 10–20 m high) are fatal. Always hold handrails, wear non-slip safety boots, and never rush on CHP walkways. Conveyor drive panels operate at medium voltage (3.3 kV or 6.6 kV in large plants, 415 V in smaller). Control panels, junction boxes, and local isolators are located along conveyor routes. Never open an electrical panel without a qualified electrician present and without following Lockout-Tagout (LOTO) procedures. Water from coal spillage near electrical panels is extremely dangerous.

text_chunks.title: Safety और Hazard Awareness
text_chunks.content: Safety और Hazard Awareness Belt conveyor एक विशाल machine है जो आपसे बहुत तेज़ चलती है और बहुत ज़्यादा ताकतवर है। यह आपको नहीं देखती। आपको ही इसे देखना होगा — हर बार, हर shift में। Belt Conveyor एक very high-energy machine है — thousands of tonnes of coal हर घंटे move करती है, कभी-कभी 3.5 m/s की speed से। CHP एक ऐसा environment है जहाँ negligence — चाहे एक पल की ही हो — life-altering consequences दे सकती है। यह section आपको primary hazards और उनसे बचाव के तरीकों से परिचित कराता है।

text_chunks.title: Transfer Between Conveyors (Transfer Point)
text_chunks.content: Transfer Between Conveyors (Transfer Point) Where: Transfer tower — where coal discharges from BC-1 and loads onto BC-2 through a chute. What is critical here: The trajectory of coal through the chute must be matched to the receiving belt speed and direction. The coal must land centrally on BC-2. The chute must be free of blockage. Chute liners (wear-resistant steel plates) must be intact. Deflector plates must direct coal accurately. This is the highest-risk location in the entire CHP. Blockages here can back-fill the chute, causing BC-1 overload. Spillage from here falls from height. Dust is at maximum. Confined space entry here requires a formal permit.

text_chunks.title: Transfer Between Conveyors (Transfer Point)
text_chunks.content: Transfer Between Conveyors (Transfer Point) कहाँ है: Transfer tower — जहाँ BC-1 से coal discharge होती है और chute के through BC-2 पर load होती है। यहाँ क्या critical है: Chute से गुज़रने वाली coal का trajectory receiving belt की speed और direction के साथ match होना चाहिए। Coal को BC-2 पर centrally land करना चाहिए। Chute blockage-free होनी चाहिए। Chute liners (wear-resistant steel plates) intact होने चाहिए। Deflector plates coal को accurately direct करें। यह पूरे CHP में सबसे high-risk location है। यहाँ blockages chute को back-fill कर सकती हैं, जिससे BC-1 overload होती है। यहाँ से spillage height से गिरती है। Dust maximum होती है। यहाँ confined space entry के लिए formal permit ज़रूरी है।

text_chunks.title: Your First Site Visit – What to Observe & What to Look For
text_chunks.content: Your First Site Visit – What to Observe & What to Look For Your first site visit is not a tour — it is a structured observation exercise. For every component you studied in this course, there is a physical object in front of you. Treat it like matching a textbook diagram to a real machine, component by component. Now that you understand the system theoretically, you need to translate that knowledge to what you will actually see, hear, and smell when you walk into the Coal Handling Plant for the first time. This guide prepares you for that transition, so you do not feel overwhelmed or miss important details. Site Visit Observation Sequence – Walk the Conveyor Like an Engineer STEP 1 Start at the Feed Point (Tail End) Observe loading STEP 2 Walk Along One Side of Belt Check belt & idlers STEP 3 Observe Drive / Head End Check discharge STEP 4 Look at Safety Devices EPC, sway switches STEP 5 Visit Transfer Tower (outside) Observe from safe zone STEP 6 – REFLECT & REPORT Note all abnormalities observed. Discuss with supervisor. NEVER act on abnormalities independently. ⛔ NEVER do this on your first visit: Do not touch, adjust, or interfere with any equipment — observe only.

text_chunks.content: इस Course में आप क्या सीखोगे ✓ Boiler तक continuous fuel supply में conveyor system का role समझना। ✓ सारे major conveyor components identify करना और उनका system में क्या काम है यह समझना। ✓ Visualize करना कि coal, unloading point (wagon tippler) से boiler bunker तक कैसे travel करती है। ✓ Belt conveyor में motion, load carrying, और tension balance का mechanism समझना। ✓ यह पहचानना कि capacity limits system stability और plant performance को कैसे affect करती हैं। ✓ High-risk zones जैसे transfer points, drive pulleys, और rotating parts के बारे में awareness develop करना। ✓ Upstream systems जैसे wagon tippler, conveyor behaviour को सीधे कैसे affect करता है, यह समझना।

text_chunks.title: यह Course कैसे इस्तेमाल करें
text_chunks.content: यह Course कैसे इस्तेमाल करें यह course इसलिए बनाया गया है ताकि आप Coal Handling Plant के belt conveyor system की पूरी mental picture बना सकें — site पर जाने से पहले। सोचिए जैसे पूरा system अपने दिमाग में download कर रहे हों, ताकि जब आप physically वहाँ पहुँचें, तो हर चीज़ पहचान सकें, उसका reason समझ सकें, और यह भी जान सकें कि खतरा कहाँ है। यह सिर्फ एक context और awareness course है। इसमें यह नहीं बताया गया कि कोई भी equipment कैसे start, stop, या operate करते हैं। आप कभी भी कोई भी operational action अकेले attempt मत करना — plant management से formal training और authorization लेने के बाद ही करना। यह course complete करने के बाद आप Coal Handling Plant में walk कर सकोगे, belt conveyor system के हर major component को identify कर सकोगे, power generation में उसका role समझोगे, और — सबसे important — hazardous zones और ऐसे behaviours पहचान सकोगे जो आपको या दूसरों को injury दे सकते हैं।

text_blocks.title: Instrumentation & Safety Devices on the Conveyor
text_blocks.content: Instrumentation & Safety Devices on the Conveyor Think of instrumentation as the conveyor's nervous system — sensors spread across the full length that continuously sense abnormal conditions and either warn operators or automatically stop the machine before a small problem becomes a catastrophe. A belt conveyor in a modern Coal Handling Plant is fitted with numerous sensors, switches, and protective devices along its entire length. These are not optional extras — they are mandatory safety and operational requirements under Indian Electricity Rules, factory safety regulations, and plant operating procedures. As an intern, you will see these devices everywhere on the conveyor. Knowing what each one does is essential. MOVING BELT TAIL PULLEY DRIVE PULLEY M ━━ EMERGENCY PULL CORD (Both Sides, Full Length) ━━ EPC EPC EPC BSW Belt Sway Switch BSW ZSS SPD Zero Speed / Underspeed Switch BW WEIGH Belt Weigher (Load cell) CBD CHUTE Chute Blocked Detector 🔥 Thermal/ Fire Detector Return Strand EPC = Emergency Pull Cord BSW = Belt Sway Switch ZSS = Zero Speed Switch BW = Belt Weigher CBD = Chute Blocked Detector 🔥 = Fire Detector

text_blocks.title: Transfer Points & Flow Behaviour
text_blocks.content: Transfer Points & Flow Behaviour A transfer point is like a controlled handover baton pass — coal must land precisely on the next belt. Any miss, blockage, or misalignment at this point disrupts the entire downstream flow. Wherever coal moves from one conveyor to the next — or from a hopper to a conveyor — there is a transfer point . These are not minor connections; they are among the most critical and most hazardous locations in the entire Coal Handling Plant. Understanding what happens at a transfer point is essential before entering the CHP. BC-1 (Upper Conveyor) Coal on BC-1 Head Pulley TRANSFER CHUTE (guides coal) ↓ Coal falls here BC-2 (Lower Conveyor) Impact Zone Coal on BC-2 ⚠ DUST ⚠ Spillage ⚠ Spillage ⚠ BLOCKAGE RISK Wet/sticky coal can block chute Coal must land centrally on BC-2 belt. Any deviation → spillage or belt drift.

text_blocks.title: What Can Go Wrong at a Transfer Point
text_blocks.content: What Can Go Wrong at a Transfer Point Problem | Cause | Consequence ; Chute Blockage | Wet, fine, or sticky coal accumulates inside the chute and sticks to walls, eventually bridging across. | Coal backs up onto BC-1, causing it to overload. If blockage is not cleared quickly, the conveyor trips. ; Spillage | Coal falls outside the belt edges due to misaligned chute, worn skirt boards, or over-speed discharge. | Accumulation of coal on walkways and structure — slipping hazard, fire risk from dust, structural overloading. ; Dust Generation | Free-fall of coal creates turbulent air that carries fine coal particles. Longer drop height = more dust. | Respiratory hazard, reduced visibility, fire and explosion risk from coal dust cloud. ; Belt Damage at Impact | Large coal lumps falling from height impact the belt at the transfer point, especially if impact idlers are worn. | Belt cover damage, gouging, or even belt puncture — leading to belt failure. ; Off-centre Loading | Coal does not land centrally on BC-2 due to incorrect chute alignment or spillage plate wear. | Belt drifts to one side → edge damage → spillage → potential belt damage against structure. Transfer towers are enclosed structures at junctions between conveyors. They are high-dust, confined-space environments with active machinery on multiple levels. Entry requires a Confined Space Entry Permit, dust mask, and must always be done with a buddy. Never enter during conveyor operation without a specific maintenance permit.

text_blocks.title: Safety Device Reference Guide
text_blocks.content: Safety Device Reference Guide Device | Location on Conveyor | Function | Response When Activated ; Emergency Pull Cord (EPC) | Both sides, full length of conveyor, approximately every 30–50 m | Allows any person anywhere along the conveyor to immediately stop it in an emergency by pulling the rope/wire | Immediate emergency stop of conveyor drive motor. Conveyor cannot restart until EPC is reset and root cause investigated. ; Belt Sway Switch (BSW) | Both sides, spaced every 50–75 m along carry and return strand | Detects lateral drift of the belt beyond a set limit. Has two positions: first position = alarm; second position = trip. | First activation: Alarm in control room. Second (greater drift): Conveyor trip. Prevents belt edge from contacting steel structure. ; Zero Speed Switch (ZSS) | Tail pulley shaft or on a return idler | Monitors belt speed. Detects if the belt has stopped (zero speed) while the motor is still running — indicating belt slip. | Conveyor trip + alarm. Prevents drive pulley from running against a stationary belt (which causes fire from friction). ; Belt Weigher (BW) | Fixed location on the conveyor, typically mid-span | Measures the weight of coal on the belt per unit length using load cells. Calculates instantaneous TPH and cumulative tonnes. | Data sent to control room / DCS. No trip — provides operational data. High load may trigger an alarm. ; Chute Blocked Detector (CBD) | Inside transfer chutes at transfer points | Detects when coal has accumulated and blocked the chute (using vibration probe, ultrasonic, or paddle switch). | Alarm in control room. May automatically stop upstream feeder to prevent further coal accumulation. ; Thermal / Fire Detector | Inside conveyor galleries (tunnels) and transfer towers | Detects elevated temperature indicating a developing fire. Linear heat detection cable runs along the belt gallery roof. | Fire alarm. Conveyor trip. Activation of fire suppression system (CO₂ or water mist). Control room alert. ; Underspeed Switch | Drive shaft area | Detects if belt is running slower than designed speed (but not zero). Indicates overloading or drive slip developing. | Alarm → trip if underspeed persists. Allows early intervention before full slippage occurs. ; Motor Overload Relay (OLR) | Motor control centre (MCC) / switchgear panel | Monitors motor current. If the motor draws current above the rated limit for a set time (indicating overload), it trips. | Motor trip + alarm. Conveyor stops. Investigation required to identify overload cause before restart. When you walk a conveyor on site, you will see red ropes, yellow boxes, and small switches mounted on the frame at regular intervals — these are all part of this safety system. You will hear terms like "BSW trip," "ZSS alarm," or "EPC activation" on the radio constantly. Now you know exactly what each term means, what triggered it, and what the plant team needs to do in response. On some plants, under production pressure, well-meaning but incorrect actions include bypassing a belt sway switch that keeps tripping, disabling a chute blocked detector that gives "false" alarms, or tying off an EPC that was accidentally pulled. This is an extremely dangerous practice. Every safety device bypass removes one layer of protection from the system. Multiple bypasses create a condition where a fatal accident can occur without any warning. As an intern, if you are ever asked to bypass a safety device, immediately consult your supervisor. Document it. Never accept it as routine.

text_blocks.title: Safety & Hazard Awareness
text_blocks.content: Safety & Hazard Awareness Moving machinery + bulk material + confined spaces = continuous risk. Most conveyor accidents happen not because of complexity but because someone was not aware of where the danger was. You do not need to be doing anything wrong to be injured near a conveyor. You simply need to be in the wrong place, distracted, or unaware of what is moving around you. The conveyor does not slow down for you. It does not have a sensor that detects a human body near it. It will continue running at full speed regardless. Your awareness is your protection. MOVING BELT (entire length is a hazard) TAIL PULLEY 🔴 PINCH ZONE Entanglement risk DRIVE PULLEY 🔴 PINCH + NIP ZONE High-torque crush risk 🟠 FEED POINT Impact hazard Dust cloud 🟠 TRANSFER POINT Spillage, blockage Confined space 🟡 BELT SURFACE Never touch/step on moving belt 🟡 Return strand — carryback coal falls here — slip hazard below ☁ Dust cloud ☁ Dust cloud ━━━ Emergency Pull Cord (full length) — Pull anywhere to STOP conveyor ━━━ HAZARD ZONE LEGEND RED = Extreme danger (pinch/nip/crush) — Mandatory guarding required ORANGE = High hazard (spillage, blockage, dust, confined space) — Permit required YELLOW = Caution zone (moving belt, carryback, slipping) — Stay clear, PPE required

text_blocks.title: Hazard-by-Hazard Analysis
text_blocks.content: Hazard-by-Hazard Analysis Pulleys rotate continuously at high speed. The nip point — where the belt meets the pulley — has an extremely small gap that closes in milliseconds. A finger, loose clothing, or hair entering this gap will be drawn in with full motor force before any human reaction is possible. Guards (physical covers) must always be in place over all pulleys. If a guard is missing — report it immediately and do not approach the pulley. The belt surface itself is a hazard. Loose clothing, gloves, tools, or anything trailing near the belt can be instantly grabbed and pulled in. Belt speed (1.5–2.5 m/s) is faster than human reflex. This type of accident typically results in degloving injuries, crush injuries, or fatalities. Rule: always wear close-fitting PPE near conveyors. Never lean over a running belt. At transfer points, coal falls from one conveyor to the next. Large coal lumps weighing several kilograms can bounce or be thrown sideways if a blockage or imbalance occurs. Standing below or beside an active chute is extremely dangerous. Transfer towers also have open floors and structural walkways at multiple levels — falling coal from one level can injure personnel on a lower level. Fine coal dust generated at transfer points, feed points, and from carryback is a dual hazard. Respiratory: Coal dust causes coal worker's pneumoconiosis (CWP/"black lung") with long-term exposure. Always wear a P2/P3 dust mask in dusty areas. Fire: Coal dust suspended in air at concentrations above the Lower Explosive Limit (LEL) can ignite from a spark or hot surface. Accumulated coal dust on hot surfaces (like a seized idler or a slipping belt) can also self-ignite. Coal spillage on walkways creates an extremely slippery surface, especially when wet. Carryback coal falls from the return strand onto the floor below the conveyor. Structural platforms, stairs, and walkways in CHP are often narrow and positioned close to moving equipment. Falls from elevated walkways (transfer towers can be 10–20 m high) are fatal. Always hold handrails, wear non-slip safety boots, and never rush on CHP walkways. Conveyor drive panels operate at medium voltage (3.3 kV or 6.6 kV in large plants, 415 V in smaller). Control panels, junction boxes, and local isolators are located along conveyor routes. Never open an electrical panel without a qualified electrician present and without following Lockout-Tagout (LOTO) procedures. Water from coal spillage near electrical panels is extremely dangerous.

text_blocks.content: 3. Safety Devices — आपकी जान बचाने वाले Instruments Belt Conveyor (Loaded Direction) EPC Rope (पूरी length में) EPC EPC EPC EPC EPC BSW BSW ZSS Speed Belt Weigher EPC: कहीं से भी खींचें → तुरंत stop ZSS: Speed drop → auto trip BSW: Belt drift → alarm → trip Belt Weigher: TPH → control room data Safety Device | काम क्या करता है | कब Trip होता है ; Emergency Pull Cord (EPC) | पूरी conveyor length में rope; कहीं से भी खींचें — instant stop | Manual pull; self-latching — investigation के बाद ही restart ; Belt Sway Switch (BSW) | Belt का lateral drift detect करता है | Stage 1: alarm; Stage 2: conveyor trip। हर 25–30 m पर। ; Zero Speed Switch (ZSS) | Belt speed monitor करता है | Speed rated से 70–80% से कम → 3 sec बाद trip ; Belt Weigher | Real-time TPH measure करता है | Trip नहीं — data control room को भेजता है ; Chute Blocked Detector | Chute fill-up detect करता है | Paddle stop / RF change → upstream belt/feeder trip ; Thermal / Fire Detector | Temperature rise या flame detect करता है | Rate-of-rise +8°C/min या fixed 68/93°C → Fire Alarm trip

text_blocks.title: Safety और Hazard Awareness
text_blocks.content: Safety और Hazard Awareness Belt conveyor एक विशाल machine है जो आपसे बहुत तेज़ चलती है और बहुत ज़्यादा ताकतवर है। यह आपको नहीं देखती। आपको ही इसे देखना होगा — हर बार, हर shift में। Belt Conveyor एक very high-energy machine है — thousands of tonnes of coal हर घंटे move करती है, कभी-कभी 3.5 m/s की speed से। CHP एक ऐसा environment है जहाँ negligence — चाहे एक पल की ही हो — life-altering consequences दे सकती है। यह section आपको primary hazards और उनसे बचाव के तरीकों से परिचित कराता है।
